prompt_sets.name: Cornell Format
prompt_sets.text:
You are helping me build a high-fidelity review for ONE concept from my board exam preparation. Stay strictly inside this concept; do not review the whole subject.

{concept}

TASK
Make a reviewer for this concept encompassing most if not all of the necessary equations, concepts, and algorithms. I want you to make an HTML file containing a synthesis of the concepts that further encompass this concept from first principles. 

I want the reviewer to be formatted based on the Cornell note taking system conducive to implement the 5R system (Record, Reduce, Recite, Reflect, Review). Take inspiration in this description:


🧱 The 3-Part Scientifically Proven Template

To format a reviewer that aligns with how the human brain processes, encodes, and retrieves information, structure every topic or chapter using this three-part format:

1. The Cue & Question Column (Left 30% of the Page)

• What it is: A narrow column reserved for keywords, high-yield questions, or prompts.
• The Science: Retrieval Practice & Testing Effect. Looking at a question rather than a statement forces your brain to actively pull information out of long-term memory, which strengthens neural pathways far better than rereading.
• Example: "What are the 3 stages of cellular respiration and where do they occur?


2. The Core Synthesis Block (Right 70% of the Page)

• What it is: The section containing answers to the left-column cues. It must be heavily structured using Concept Maps, Tables, or Timelines instead of blocks of prose. Information should be broken down into:
	• AO1 (Knowledge): Core facts and definitions.
	• AO3 (Evaluation/Application): Strengths, weaknesses, and real-world examples
The Science: Dual Coding & Elaborative Interrogation. The human brain processes visual spatial layouts and text through separate channels. Organizing info into trees or matrices prevents "illusions of competence" (the false feeling that you know the material just because it looks familiar).


3. The Active Reflection & Blurting Box (Bottom of the Page)

• What it is: A blank space or a dedicated prompt section at the bottom of the topic sheet. It should feature low-stakes active retrieval prompts (like a mini multiple-choice or short definition box) and a blank area to "blurt" (write down everything you remember from memory before checking your notes)
The Science: Metacognitive Monitoring & Spaced Repetition. Leaving space to track confidence levels and record mistakes in a different color ink helps the brain realize what it actually forgot, correcting the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve


RULES
- Use only standard, verifiable facts for this subject. If something is uncertain, say so.
- If a bank correct answer above looks wrong, ambiguous or condition-dependent, tell me instead of rationalizing it.
- Base the Trap lines on MY answers above, not on generic advice.

concept_cards.front: Ethoxide or hydroxide (strong base) with a 3° alkyl halide, and with a 2° alkyl halide: which mechanisms?
concept_cards.back: 3° halide + strong base = E2 only (no SN2 because of steric hindrance, no E1 because E1 needs a weak base). 2° halide + strong base/good nucleophile = SN2 and E2 compete (E2 usually major). E1/SN1 need a weak base or nucleophile, a polar protic solvent, and usually heat. With a small base like EtO⁻, E2 gives the most substituted alkene (Zaitsev). Count substituents on the C=C to choose: tetrasubstituted beats trisubstituted.
concept_cards.trap: I picked E1 for ethoxide + tert-butyl bromide (#58) and E1 and E2 for 2-iodohexane + ethoxide (#59). Strong base means no E1. In #55 I chose the trisubstituted alkene (D) over the tetrasubstituted 2,3-dimethyl-2-hexene (B), so check the locants and count the substituents.

concept_cards.front: Cl₂ (or Br₂) adds to 1-butene. Where do the halogens go, and what about HCl?
concept_cards.back: X₂ adds through a halonium ion with anti addition, one X on each alkene carbon, giving a vicinal dihalide: CH₃CH₂CHClCH₂Cl. Markovnikov applies only to HX (H goes to the carbon with more H's, X to the more substituted carbon).
concept_cards.trap: I picked the geminal CH₃CH₂CCl₂CH₃ (#75). Both Cl's on one carbon is never the result of X₂ addition.

concept_cards.front: Ozonolysis of an alkene (O₃, then Me₂S or Zn): what does each alkene carbon become?
concept_cards.back: The C=C is cleaved and each carbon becomes C=O. A carbon with one H becomes an aldehyde, and a carbon with no H (two alkyl groups) becomes a ketone. Reductive workup stops at aldehydes/ketones; oxidative workup (H₂O₂) turns aldehydes into carboxylic acids. Unbranched heptenes (1-, 2-, or 3-heptene) give two different aldehydes.
concept_cards.trap: I picked an aldehyde and a ketone (#77). A ketone needs a trisubstituted or tetrasubstituted alkene carbon, which an unbranched alkene doesn't have.

concept_cards.front: Name the reaction from its cue: (a) conjugated diene + alkene to a cyclohexene; (b) aldehyde/ketone + phosphorus ylide to an alkene; (c) ketone + primary amine.
concept_cards.back: (a) Diels-Alder, a concerted [4+2] cycloaddition. (b) Wittig reaction, C=O becomes C=C (Ph₃P=O is a by-product). (c) Imine (Schiff base), C=N–R. A secondary amine gives an enamine instead.
concept_cards.trap: I only guessed these (#113, #114, #87). Tie each name to its cue word: [4+2] means Diels-Alder, ylide means Wittig, primary amine means imine.

concept_cards.front: Atoms per unit cell for SC, BCC, and FCC, and how do I count them?
concept_cards.back: Corner atom = 1/8, face atom = 1/2, edge atom = 1/4, body-center atom = 1. SC = 8 × 1/8 = 1. BCC = 8 × 1/8 + 1 = 2. FCC = 8 × 1/8 + 6 × 1/2 = 4.
concept_cards.trap: I answered 4 for BCC (#19). Four atoms per cell is FCC. BCC has only the 8 corners plus 1 center, which is 2.

concept_cards.front: How do I identify the crystal system, and which has the lowest symmetry?
concept_cards.back: Check edge lengths first, then angles. Cubic: a=b=c, all angles 90°. Tetragonal: a=b≠c, all 90°. Orthorhombic: a≠b≠c, all 90°. Monoclinic: a≠b≠c, two angles 90° and one (β) not 90°. Triclinic: a≠b≠c, no angle equal to 90° and all angles different, so it has the lowest symmetry. Atoms at the center or faces do not change the system (a body-centered tetragonal cell is still tetragonal).
concept_cards.trap: In #17 the base edges were both 0.35 nm, so a=b≠c is tetragonal, not orthorhombic. In #18 my note said monoclinic has all 90° angles, but that is orthorhombic. Monoclinic has one non-90° angle, so it is not the lowest symmetry.

concept_cards.front: How do I get the unit cell side a and volume from the atomic radius R for SC, BCC, and FCC?
concept_cards.back: Atoms touch along the closest-packed direction. SC: a = 2R. BCC (body diagonal): 4R = a√3, so a = 4R/√3. FCC (face diagonal): 4R = a√2, so a = 2√2·R. Volume V = a³ (cubic cell). Convert nm to m before cubing, since 1 nm³ = 10⁻²⁷ m³. Example for lead (FCC), R = 0.175 nm: a = 0.495 nm, V = 0.1213 nm³ = 1.21×10⁻²⁸ m³.
concept_cards.trap: In #23 I picked 2.67×10⁻²⁸ m³ even though my method (FCC, then a, then a³) was right, so the error was in the formula or arithmetic. Write a = 2√2·R explicitly, cube the full value of a, and check the exponent.

concept_cards.front: Miller notation: what do (hkl), [uvw], {hkl}, and <uvw> mean, and how do I get (hkl) from intercepts?
concept_cards.back: (hkl) = a specific plane, [uvw] = a specific direction, {hkl} = a family of planes, <uvw> = a family of directions. For a plane: take the intercepts on x, y, z, take reciprocals, then clear fractions. Intercepts 1, 1, 1 give reciprocals 1, 1, 1, so the plane is (111). A plane parallel to an axis has intercept ∞, so that index is 0.
concept_cards.trap: In #28 the bank lists [1 1 1] for a plane, which is direction notation. My guess note on bracket types was right. Choose the (hkl) form if it is offered, and flag the question if it is not.

concept_cards.front: Why do colligative properties occur, and what is the solvent's chemical potential at osmotic equilibrium?
concept_cards.back: A solute lowers the solvent's chemical potential: μ = μ* + RT ln x, and x < 1 makes the ln term negative. The cause is the entropy gain from mixing. Every colligative property comes from this reduction of μ of the liquid solvent. Before equilibrium, solvent flows toward the lower μ (the solution side). At osmotic equilibrium the solvent's μ is equal on both sides, because the extra pressure π on the solution side raises its μ back up to match the pure solvent.
concept_cards.trap: I picked "Change" instead of "Reduction" in #48 (the direction is specific: lowered), and "Less than" in #49. Less than describes the state before equilibrium. Any equilibrium means equal chemical potentials.

concept_cards.front: How do I find the van't Hoff factor i from a freezing point depression, and the degree of dissociation α from i?
concept_cards.back: ΔTf = i·Kf·m, so i = ΔTf / (Kf·m), with m in mol solute per kg solvent. For wt%, take x g solute in (100 - x) g solvent (100 g is a fair approximation if the solution is dilute). Kf(water) = 1.86 K·kg/mol. Dissociation: i = 1 + α(ν - 1), so α = (i - 1)/(ν - 1), where ν is the number of ions per formula unit (NaCl, ν = 2). Example (#55): 0.72 g HCl is 0.0197 mol in 0.0993 kg, so m = 0.199 mol/kg and i = 0.706/(1.86 × 0.199) = 1.91 ≈ 1.9.
concept_cards.trap: I answered 1.85 in #55 (key 1.9), even though my Kf and formula were right. Convert grams to moles using the molar mass of HCl (36.46 g/mol) and kg of solvent, and keep three significant figures before rounding.

concept_cards.front: How do I get the ebullioscopic constant Kb from Trouton's rule?
concept_cards.back: Trouton-Hildebrand-Everett: ΔHvap ≈ c·Tb with c ≈ 85-88 J/(mol·K). Kb = R·Tb²·M / ΔHvap (M in kg/mol), which simplifies to Kb = R·Tb·M / c. Use Tb in kelvin. Diethyl ether (#58): Tb = 307.75 K, M = 0.07412 kg/mol, so Kb = 8.314 × 307.75 × 0.07412 / 85 = 2.23 K·kg/mol. With c = 88 you get 2.16. Then ΔTb = i·Kb·m gives i, and α = i - 1 for ν = 2. For #60: m = 2.567 mol / 0.300 kg = 8.56 mol/kg, i ≈ 1.36, α ≈ 36%.
concept_cards.trap: I answered 1.32 in #58 (key 2.23) and 31.6% in #60 (key 36.1%). Check that Tb is in kelvin (34.6 + 273.15), M is in kg/mol, and which Trouton constant (85 or 88) the bank uses. An error in Kb carries into #60.

concept_cards.front: How do I calculate the osmotic pressure of an electrolyte solution?
concept_cards.back: van't Hoff equation: π = i·M·R·T, with M in mol/L and T in kelvin. Use R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) for atm, then multiply by 760 to get mmHg. For dilute aqueous solutions, molarity ≈ molality. Example (#56): T = 26.85 + 273.15 = 300.0 K, M ≈ 0.199 mol/L, i ≈ 1.91, so π = 1.91 × 0.199 × 0.08206 × 300.0 = 9.4 atm ≈ 7100 mmHg (the key's 7000 is the nearest option).
concept_cards.trap: I answered 4000 in #56 (key 7000). Without i the result is about 3700 mmHg, which is near my choice. For any electrolyte (HCl, NaCl), multiply by i before converting units.

concept_cards.front: What does the Clausius-Clapeyron slope dP/dT relate to, and what does Trouton's rule say about ΔS_vap?
concept_cards.back: dP/dT = ΔH_vap/(T·ΔV) = ΔS_vap/ΔV, so the slope of the vapor pressure curve is set by the entropy change of vaporization. At the boiling point ΔS_vap = ΔH_vap/T_b. Trouton's rule: ΔS_vap ≈ 85-88 J/(mol·K) for many non-associated liquids. It fails for hydrogen-bonded or polar liquids (water ≈ 109 J/(mol·K), higher) and for very low-boiling liquids like He and H₂ (lower).
concept_cards.trap: In #76 I answered "Temperature", but T is the variable in the derivative, not the property that sets the slope. In #52 I wrote that polar liquids have lower entropy yet a larger change. The liquid is more ordered, so the entropy gain on vaporizing is larger than 85-88.

concept_cards.front: What is the entropy of mixing of ideal gases, and how do I compute it?
concept_cards.back: ΔS_mix = -R Σ nᵢ ln xᵢ = -nR Σ xᵢ ln xᵢ, in J/K. It is always positive and independent of the identity of the gases. Example (#14), 2 mol N₂ + 1 mol O₂: x = 2/3 and 1/3. N₂: -2R ln(2/3) = 6.74 J/K. O₂: -1R ln(1/3) = 9.13 J/K. Total = 15.9 J/K.
concept_cards.trap: I answered 11.5 J/K in #14. That equals 2R ln 2, so check that both gases are included, that x is the mole fraction (not the mole ratio), and that n is the total moles (3, not 2).

concept_cards.front: How do I get the entropy change of heating at constant pressure?
concept_cards.back: ΔS = ∫(Cp/T)dT = m·Cp·ln(T₂/T₁) for constant Cp, with T in kelvin. Per unit mass: ΔS = Cp ln(T₂/T₁) in kJ/(kg·K). Example (#84): 1 × ln(313.15/293.15) = 0.066 kJ/kg·K. For constant volume use Cv instead of Cp.
concept_cards.trap: In #84 I chose 0.022, and the bank's key of 0.034 doesn't match my calculation either. Convert °C to K first (20 °C = 293.15 K). Using the Celsius numbers, ln(40/20) = 0.693, is a common error.

concept_cards.front: What is ΔS for an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas?
concept_cards.back: ΔS = Q_rev/T = nR ln(V₂/V₁), in J/K. ΔU = 0 for an ideal gas at constant T, so Q = W. Example (#70): ΔS = 500 J / 350 K = 1.43 J/K. Q/T works directly when the heat is given as reversibly absorbed; nR ln(V₂/V₁) needs n.
concept_cards.trap: I guessed #70. When Q and T are given, divide them. When only volumes are given, you need n.

concept_cards.front: How do I calculate elastic elongation from an applied stress?
concept_cards.back: Hooke's law: σ = E·ε, so ε = σ/E and ΔL = ε·L₀ = σ·L₀/E. Keep the units consistent: 1 GPa = 1000 MPa. Example (#39): ε = 315 / 107,000 = 2.94×10⁻³ (dimensionless), and ΔL = 2.94×10⁻³ × 250 mm = 0.74 mm. Valid only while the deformation is entirely elastic.
concept_cards.trap: I answered 0.55 mm in #39 even though my method was right. Convert E to MPa (107 GPa = 107,000 MPa) before dividing, then multiply by the original length in mm. Check that the answer is a small fraction of L₀, about 0.3% here.

concept_cards.front: Yield strength vs. tensile strength: where is each on the engineering stress-strain curve?
concept_cards.back: Yield strength is the stress where plastic (permanent) deformation begins, at the end of the linear elastic region. Tensile strength (ultimate tensile strength, UTS) is the maximum stress on the engineering curve, the peak just before necking begins. After the peak, the engineering stress falls while the material necks until fracture.
concept_cards.trap: In #42 I picked yield strength. The question said "maximum stress" and "maximum point," and the maximum point is the peak (UTS), not the start of plasticity. Match the keyword: onset of permanent deformation means yield, maximum stress means tensile strength.

concept_cards.front: Toughness vs. resilience vs. strength: which one is energy absorption, and over what range?
concept_cards.back: Toughness is the energy absorbed up to fracture, the total area under the stress-strain curve (elastic plus plastic), in J/m³. Resilience is the energy absorbed in the elastic range only, the area under the elastic region, U_r = σ_y²/(2E), and it is recovered when unloaded. Strength is the stress a material can withstand (a stress, in MPa), not an energy.
concept_cards.trap: In #43 I picked "strength" for energy absorption, and in #44 I picked "toughness" for the elastic range only. Energy over the whole curve is toughness, and energy over the elastic range only is resilience. Strength is never energy.

concept_cards.front: Why are ceramics brittle?
concept_cards.back: Ceramics have ionic and covalent bonds that are strong and directional. Dislocation motion (slip) is very difficult, because slip would bring like-charged ions together in ionic solids and break covalent bonds. Without plastic deformation to blunt flaws, cracks grow and the material fractures suddenly. Ceramics also have pores and microcracks that act as stress concentrators. Metals deform plastically because their metallic bonding allows slip.
concept_cards.trap: In #47 I picked grain boundaries. Metals are crystalline too, and they are ductile, so a crystalline structure by itself does not explain brittleness. Look for the bond type, which is what blocks slip.

concept_cards.front: How do I read Km and Vmax from a Lineweaver-Burk line y = b + m·x (x = 1/[S], y = 1/v)?
concept_cards.back: 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. y-intercept b = 1/Vmax, so Vmax = 1/b. Slope m = Km/Vmax, so Km = m/b = m·Vmax. x-intercept = -1/Km. Km has the units of [S], and Vmax has the units of v. Example (#79): m = 0.01738, b = 4.43×10⁻⁴, so Km = 0.01738 / 4.43×10⁻⁴ = 39.2 M.
concept_cards.trap: In #79 I answered 4.43 M, which is just the intercept. The intercept gives 1/Vmax, not Km. Divide slope by intercept.

concept_cards.front: What is the Michaelis-Menten equation, and which step is rate-determining?
concept_cards.back: E + S ⇌ ES → E + P. v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]), with Vmax = kcat[E]total and Km = (k₋₁ + kcat)/k₁. Km is the [S] at which v = Vmax/2. The rate-determining step is the catalytic step, ES → E + P (product formation, rate constant kcat). A low Km means high apparent affinity, when kcat is small relative to k₋₁.
concept_cards.trap: In #75 I chose the ES dissociation step back to substrate. That is the reverse of binding, not a step toward product. The slow step is the one that forms product.

concept_cards.front: How do competitive, noncompetitive, and uncompetitive inhibitors change Km and Vmax, and who binds the active site?
concept_cards.back: Competitive: binds the active site, Km(app) increases, Vmax unchanged (Lineweaver-Burk lines meet at the y-axis). Pure noncompetitive: binds an allosteric site, Vmax decreases, Km unchanged (lines meet at the x-axis). Uncompetitive: binds only ES, both Km and Vmax decrease (parallel lines). Active-site binders include the substrate, competitive inhibitors, and many irreversible inhibitors that covalently modify active-site residues.
concept_cards.trap: In #87 I picked only "reversible competitive inhibitor." The question asked what binds at the active site, and several answers qualify. If the options include "more than one" or "both," check every option before choosing.

concept_cards.front: What does an allosteric activator do to a sigmoidal v vs. [S] curve?
concept_cards.back: Cooperative allosteric enzymes give a sigmoidal curve (not hyperbolic). An activator stabilizes the R (relaxed, high-affinity) state: the curve shifts left (lower K₀.₅, higher apparent affinity) and becomes more hyperbolic, with Vmax usually unchanged (K-type). An inhibitor stabilizes the T (tense) state: the curve shifts right and becomes more sigmoidal. Do not use Km for sigmoidal enzymes, use K₀.₅.
concept_cards.trap: In #83 I picked only "increases binding affinity," but the key was "both A and C," so the R-state stabilization was also part of the answer. In #85 I guessed. Activator means left shift and more hyperbolic. Right shift and more sigmoidal means inhibitor.

concept_cards.front: Which greenhouse gas has a 100-year GWP of about 273, and what are the GWPs and main sources of CO₂, CH₄, and N₂O?
concept_cards.back: GWP (100-year, IPCC AR6): CO₂ = 1, CH₄ ≈ 27-30 (about 81-83 over 20 years), N₂O ≈ 273. N₂O comes from agriculture (fertilizer, manure), industry, fossil fuel and waste combustion, and wastewater treatment. CH₄ comes from livestock, landfills, rice paddies, and fossil fuel leaks. GWP is relative to CO₂ over a stated time horizon, so always check the horizon.
concept_cards.trap: I picked methane in #31 even though my note had N₂O = 273. Match the number in the question to the gas first, then read the options.

concept_cards.front: What shape is a dose-response curve for acute toxicity, and how do I compare the potency of two chemicals?
concept_cards.back: Acute (quantal) dose-response curves are S-shaped (sigmoidal): almost no response at low dose, a steep near-linear middle, and a plateau at maximum response. On a log-dose axis the curve is symmetric. Potency is compared at the same effect level, usually LD50 or ED50 (the dose giving 50% response). A lower LD50 means more toxic, and the curve is shifted to the left. The threshold is the highest dose with no effect.
concept_cards.trap: In #69 I chose a straight 45° line, but acute toxicity gives an S-curve. In #70 I chose "without a threshold" instead of the potency answer. A curve farther left (lower dose for the same effect) is the most poisonous.

concept_cards.front: A heat engine burns fuel with energy content q, mass m, and efficiency η. How do I split the energy into work and waste heat?
concept_cards.back: Q_in = m × q (convert kg to g first if q is in kJ/g). W = η × Q_in (useful work). Q_out (rejected to the surroundings) = Q_in - W = (1 - η) × Q_in. Example (#19): Q_in = 20,000 g × 35 kJ/g = 700 MJ. W = 0.35 × 700 = 245 MJ. Q_out = 0.65 × 700 = 455 MJ ≈ 450 MJ.
concept_cards.trap: In #19 I answered 250 MJ, which is the work output (245 MJ). "Released to the surroundings" means the waste heat, 65% of the input, not 35%.

concept_cards.front: Which common fossil fuel has the highest carbon content, and how do the fossil fuels compare in H:C ratio?
concept_cards.back: Coal has the highest carbon fraction (anthracite above 90% C), and the lowest hydrogen content per carbon. Liquid fuels (gasoline, diesel) are about 85-87% C and are hydrocarbons with more H. Natural gas (mostly CH₄) is the richest in H, about 75% C by mass. A higher C:H ratio means more CO₂ per unit of energy, so coal has the most pronounced environmental effects of the three.
concept_cards.trap: In #8 I picked diesel, even though my note said liquid fuels have more hydrogen and less carbon. "Highest carbon content" means the lowest H:C, which is coal.

concept_cards.front: What are the dimensions of point, line, surface, and volume defects, and which one comes from imperfect packing during crystallization?
concept_cards.back: Point defects are 0-D (vacancy, self-interstitial, substitutional or interstitial impurity). Line defects are 1-D (dislocations: edge, screw, mixed). Surface or planar defects are 2-D (grain boundaries, twin boundaries, free surfaces, stacking faults). Volume defects are 3-D (voids, pores, cracks, precipitates, inclusions). Imperfect packing of atoms during crystallization gives point defects such as vacancies and interstitials.
concept_cards.trap: In #32 I wrote that a point defect is 1-D and picked "volume." Point defects are 0-D, and the 1-D defect is the dislocation. Volume defects are voids and inclusions, not packing errors at the atomic level.

concept_cards.front: How does the equilibrium vacancy concentration depend on temperature, and what does it not depend on?
concept_cards.back: Nv = N·exp(-Qv/kT), with N = total atomic sites per unit volume, Qv = vacancy formation energy, k = Boltzmann constant (8.617×10⁻⁵ eV/atom·K, or 1.38×10⁻²³ J/K), and T in kelvin. Vacancies increase exponentially with temperature and decrease with a higher formation energy. Atomic mass does not appear in the formula (it only enters through N via the density).
concept_cards.trap: In #37 I picked increasing atomic mass. The formula has T in the exponent and no mass term. "Vacancy defect increases with..." means temperature.

concept_cards.front: Schottky vs. Frenkel defect: what is each, and which one keeps the crystal neutral by vacancy pairs?
concept_cards.back: Schottky: a missing cation and a missing anion (in the ratio of the formula, so the crystal stays neutral). Both ions leave their sites and go to the surface, so the density drops. Typical in NaCl and CsCl, where the ions are similar in size. Frenkel: an ion (usually the smaller cation) leaves its site and sits in an interstitial position, giving a vacancy-interstitial pair. The density is unchanged. Typical in AgCl and ZnS.
concept_cards.trap: In #33 I picked Frenkel for "cation/anion vacancy clusters." Frenkel has an interstitial, and Schottky has only vacancies. Look for the cue word: vacancy pair means Schottky, interstitial means Frenkel.

concept_cards.front: How do I calculate the number of vacancies per m³ from Q, density, and atomic weight?
concept_cards.back: Step 1: N = Nₐ·ρ/A (atoms/cm³), then multiply by 10⁶ to get atoms/m³. Step 2: T in kelvin (°C + 273). Step 3: Nv = N·exp(-Q/kT) with Q in eV and k = 8.617×10⁻⁵ eV/K. Example (#34, Cu at 1000 °C): N = 6.022×10²³ × 8.4 / 63.5 = 7.97×10²² atoms/cm³ = 7.97×10²⁸ atoms/m³. Q/kT = 0.9/(8.617×10⁻⁵ × 1273) = 8.20. Nv = 7.97×10²⁸ × 2.74×10⁻⁴ = 2.2×10²⁵ atoms/m³.
concept_cards.trap: In #34 I guessed even though I had the right formula. Convert °C to K, use k in eV/K when Q is in eV, and convert cm³ to m³ (×10⁶) before the exponential. Check that Nv is a tiny fraction of N (about 3×10⁻⁴ here).

concept_cards.front: What is the two-point Clausius-Clapeyron formula for ΔH_vap, and what units and constants does it need?
concept_cards.back: ln(P₂/P₁) = -(ΔH_vap/R)(1/T₂ - 1/T₁), so ΔH_vap = R·ln(P₂/P₁) / (1/T₁ - 1/T₂). T must be in kelvin. P can be in any unit, as long as both pressures use the same one. R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) for J or kJ answers, 1.987 cal/(mol·K) for cal answers. It assumes ΔH is constant over the range, the vapor is ideal, and the liquid volume is negligible. Example (#42): ln(141.801/52.301) = 0.997; 1/T₁ - 1/T₂ = 2.513×10⁻⁴ K⁻¹; ΔH = 8.314 × 0.997 / 2.513×10⁻⁴ = 33.0 kJ/mol.
concept_cards.trap: In #42 I answered 37 kJ/mol (key 33). Convert nothing else, but check three things: that I used 1/T (not T), that the pressure ratio is P₂/P₁ with matching order for the temperatures, and that the exponent in 1/T is right (10⁻⁴, not 10⁻³).

concept_cards.front: With a table of 5 vapor-pressure points, how do I estimate ΔH_vap?
concept_cards.back: Plot ln P against 1/T (T in kelvin). The line has slope = -ΔH_vap/R, so ΔH_vap = -slope × R. For a quick estimate, use the two end points of the table, as the slope is nearly constant. A best-fit line over all points gives a slightly different answer. Example (#45): ln(355.343/55.364) = 1.859; Δ(1/T) = -3.617×10⁻⁴ K⁻¹; slope = -5140 K; ΔH = 5140 × 8.314 = 42.7 kJ/mol ≈ 43.
concept_cards.trap: In #45 I answered 45 kJ/mol (key 43). Convert °C to K (add 273.15) before taking reciprocals, and use ln (natural log), not log₁₀. If I use log₁₀, the slope is -ΔH/(2.303R). Pick the nearest option, because small differences come from rounding of 1/T.

concept_cards.front: What is the pressure at a "normal" boiling or sublimation point, and how do I use it in a ΔH calculation?
concept_cards.back: "Normal" means the pressure is 1 atm = 760 torr = 760 mmHg = 1.01325 bar. If a question gives one vapor pressure at one temperature plus the normal boiling or sublimation point, then the second point is (1 atm, T_normal). Example (#44, CO₂ sublimation): point 1 = (76.7 mmHg, 170.15 K); point 2 = (760 mmHg, 194.65 K). ΔH_sub = 1.987 × ln(760/76.7) / (1/170.15 - 1/194.65) = 6160 cal/mol.
concept_cards.trap: In #44 I answered 6610 (key 6160), which is the same digits swapped. Write the final number back against the intermediate values (ln ratio ≈ 2.29, Δ(1/T) ≈ 7.4×10⁻⁴) before choosing an option. Also check that the answer is in cal/mol, not kJ/mol, so R = 1.987.

concept_cards.front: Br₂ has a normal boiling point of 58.8 °C and a vapor pressure of 0.287 bar at 25 °C. How do I find the average ΔH_vap, and what's the pressure trap?
concept_cards.back: Point 1 = (0.287 bar, 298.15 K). Point 2 = (1 atm = 1.01325 bar, 331.95 K). ΔH = 8.314 × ln(1.01325/0.287) / (1/298.15 - 1/331.95) = 8.314 × 1.262 / 3.415×10⁻⁴ ≈ 30.7 kJ/mol ≈ 31. Using exactly 1 bar for the normal boiling point gives ≈ 30.4. P must be in the same unit at both points (convert 1 atm to bar here). The result is an average over the range.
concept_cards.trap: I guessed #43. The pressure at the normal boiling point is hidden in the wording, so write it down as a second data point before anything else. A pressure in bar and a normal boiling pressure in atm or torr must be converted to one unit.

concept_cards.front: First-order linear y' + P(x)y = Q(x): what is the integrating factor and the first thing to check?
concept_cards.back: Write the equation with the coefficient of y' equal to 1, then μ = exp(∫P dx), taking C = 0. Multiplying gives (μy)' = μQ. Example (#22): y' - y tan x = sin x, so P = -tan x. ∫-tan x dx = -(-ln|cos x|) = ln|cos x|, so μ = cos x. Check: cos x·y' - sin x·y = (y cos x)' = sin x cos x.
concept_cards.trap: I picked -cos(x) in #22. The minus sign in P = -tan x is part of P, and the two minus signs cancel in ∫-tan x dx = ln|cos x|. An exp(...) can never produce a negative value, so the answer is cos x.

concept_cards.front: Bernoulli equation y' + P(x)y = Q(x)yⁿ: how do I get the integrating factor?
concept_cards.back: Substitute v = y^(1-n). Then v' + (1-n)P v = (1-n)Q, which is linear in v, and μ = exp(∫(1-n)P dx). Example (#25): n = 2, v = 1/y, so v' - (4/x)v = -x³. μ = exp(∫-4/x dx) = exp(-4 ln x) = x⁻⁴ = 1/x⁴. Check: (v/x⁴)' = -1/x.
concept_cards.trap: I picked 1/x³ in #25 even though my linearized form was right. The power of x comes from P = 4/x, multiplied by (1-n) = -1. It does not come from the x³ on the right side.

concept_cards.front: Non-exact M dx + N dy = 0: when is μ a function of x only, and what is it?
concept_cards.back: First test exactness: if M_y ≠ N_x, try μ(x). If (M_y - N_x)/N depends on x only, then μ = exp(∫(M_y - N_x)/N dx). Example (#14): M = x² + y² + 3, N = -2xy, so M_y = 2y and N_x = -2y. (M_y - N_x)/N = 4y/(-2xy) = -2/x, so μ = exp(-2 ln x) = x⁻² = 1/x². Check: after multiplying, M_y = N_x = 2y/x².
concept_cards.trap: I answered -2/x in #14, which is the integrand and not the integrating factor. The last step is exp of the integral, and a quick check is that M_y = N_x after multiplying.

concept_cards.front: Non-exact M dx + N dy = 0: when is μ a function of y only, and what is it?
concept_cards.back: If (N_x - M_y)/M depends on y only, then μ = exp(∫(N_x - M_y)/M dy). The numerator flips compared with the μ(x) case: μ(x) uses (M_y - N_x)/N, and μ(y) uses (N_x - M_y)/M. Example (#16): M = y⁴ + 2y, N = xy³ + 2y⁴ - 4x. N_x - M_y = (y³ - 4) - (4y³ + 2) = -3(y³ + 2). Dividing by M = y(y³ + 2) gives -3/y, so μ = y⁻³ = 1/y³.
concept_cards.trap: I picked y³ in #16, which is the result of using (M_y - N_x)/M and getting +3/y. Memory aid: the divisor is the coefficient of the differential I am NOT integrating over (N for μ(x), M for μ(y)), and the numerator is (derivative of the other coefficient) minus (derivative of the divisor's own coefficient)... verify by checking M_y = N_x after multiplying.

concept_cards.front: What are the routes of entry of toxicants into the body, and which is the main one in the workplace?
concept_cards.back: Inhalation, ingestion, and dermal (skin) absorption. Injection is a fourth route in some texts. Inhalation is usually the most significant route for workplace chemicals. Ingestion is usually accidental (contaminated hands, food, drinks) and is preventable, for example by handwashing and not eating in the lab. If a question lists the routes separately and also offers "all of the above," the complete answer is usually the one wanted.
concept_cards.trap: In #62 I picked dermal absorption alone, though my own note said it was only one route. In #65 I picked a true statement (option C, about reducing ingestion by handwashing) when the question asked for the incorrect statement. Read whether the stem asks for true or incorrect, and check every option, including "all of the above."

concept_cards.front: What does the GHS pictogram of a person with a starburst on the chest mean, and how does it differ from the skull and crossbones and the exclamation mark?
concept_cards.back: Starburst on the chest: serious health hazard (carcinogenicity, mutagenicity, reproductive toxicity, respiratory sensitization, specific target organ toxicity, aspiration hazard). Skull and crossbones: acute toxicity, fatal or toxic. Exclamation mark: irritant, skin sensitizer, harmful (lower acute toxicity), narcotic effects. The starburst covers chronic and long-term effects, not only acute ones.
concept_cards.trap: In #44 I picked acute toxicity, but my note already said the starburst is for chronic serious hazards. Pair each symbol with its cue: skull means acute (deadly), starburst means long-term damage, exclamation mark means irritant.

concept_cards.front: Which SDS section do I check for stability, reactivity, and water-reactive or incompatible chemicals?
concept_cards.back: Section 10, Stability and reactivity (conditions to avoid, incompatible materials, hazardous decomposition products). Other key sections of the 16-section SDS: 1 identification, 2 hazard identification, 3 composition, 4 first-aid measures, 5 firefighting measures, 6 accidental release measures, 7 handling and storage, 8 exposure controls and PPE, 9 physical and chemical properties, 11 toxicological information, 14 transport, 15 regulatory.
concept_cards.trap: In #41 I picked Section 9 (physical and chemical properties) for a chemical that reacted violently with water. A violent reaction is a reactivity question, so go to Section 10. Section 9 gives data like boiling point and flash point, not what the chemical reacts with.

concept_cards.front: Which fire extinguisher class fits electrical equipment, and which fires can a CO₂ extinguisher be used on?
concept_cards.back: Traditional classes: A = ordinary combustibles (wood, paper, cloth); B = flammable liquids and gases; C = energized electrical equipment; D = combustible metals; K = cooking oils and fats. Electrical equipment (appliances, power tools, wiring) uses Class C, and the agent must be non-conductive. CO₂ is a clean, non-conductive agent used on Class B and C fires. It is not suited for Class A or D.
concept_cards.trap: In #49 and #50 I guessed. Tie each letter to its fuel: B = Bottle of liquid (flammable liquids), C = Current (electrical). CO₂ goes with B and C because it leaves no residue and doesn't conduct electricity.

concept_cards.front: How do you get the dew point of a gas mixture from its composition and total pressure?
concept_cards.back: pv = y(water) × P(total). The dew point is the temperature where Psat(water) = pv. Use consistent units (kPa or mmHg). Dry-bulb temperature does not enter, as long as it is above the dew point.
concept_cards.trap: In #68 the total pressure was 5260 mmHg and the temperature 100 °C. The working number is pv = 0.10 × 5260 = 526 mmHg, which matches Psat of water at 90 °C. You answered 72 °C, so check which pressure you used for the lookup.

concept_cards.front: Specific humidity W from temperature, total pressure and relative humidity?
concept_cards.back: pv = RH × Psat(T). Then W = 0.622 × pv / (P − pv), in kg water per kg dry air. The molar version is Y = pv / (P − pv), in mol per mol dry air. At 35 °C, Psat is about 5.63 kPa, so 40% RH gives pv ≈ 2.25 kPa and W ≈ 0.0141.
concept_cards.trap: In #73 you answered 0.025, which is about the value at ~70% RH. Compute pv first as a sanity check on the chart reading. Also keep W (per dry air) separate from vapor mole fraction y (per total gas).

concept_cards.front: Gas stream is cooled and compressed to recover a vapor (like benzene in N2). How do you set it up?
concept_cards.back: Use the inert gas as a constant basis. Find the initial vapor partial pressure (RH × Psat if given RH). Remove the required fraction of vapor. At the final temperature the gas is saturated, so pv = Psat(T_final). Then P = Psat(T_final) / y_final, where y_final = n_vapor,left / (n_inert + n_vapor,left).
concept_cards.trap: In #72 you left it blank. Don’t try to find P in one jump. Set a basis of 100 mol feed, then do the balance. Also, “percentage relative humidity” means pv/Psat. Percentage saturation (Y/Ys) gives a different number.

concept_cards.front: Mixing two humid air streams: what is conserved, and how do you get the mixed dry-bulb temperature?
concept_cards.back: On a dry-air basis, mass of dry air, mass of water (so W) and enthalpy are all conserved. Mixed W = Σ(m_da × W) / Σ m_da. Mixed h = Σ(m_da × h) / Σ m_da. Dry-bulb is then solved from h and W. Because the streams’ humidities are similar, a dry-air-weighted average of dry-bulb temperatures is a good shortcut, usually within about 0.5 degrees.
concept_cards.trap: In #87 you left it blank. Mixing is a weighted average, not a chart-only problem. Weight by dry-air mass, not by total mass. Don’t use wet-bulb temperatures in the average.

concept_cards.back: Absolute humidity

concept_cards.back: Specific humidity
